lede: S&P 500 joins the Nasdaqs at a record; oil back above $101 on Houthi attacks; Fed minutes at 2:00.

Tue close, plans to boost 2027 chip supply (Reuters)

geo_headlines: THREE RECORDS: THE S&P 500 JOINED THE NASDAQS. The S&P 500 rose 0.58% Tuesday to 7,818.93, above its August 13 record on both the close and the intraday high, its first record close in two months. The Nasdaq 100 rose 0.48% to 31,224.69 and the Nasdaq Composite 0.45% to 27,599.89, both records again; the Dow rose 0.49% but is 5.2% below its August record (Reuters, AP). **Analysts expect S&P 500 third-quarter earnings growth of about 30% (LSEG), and that is what stocks are pricing.**

YIELDS EASED, THEN FIRMED. The 10-year closed at 5.27% (-4bp) and the 2-year at 4.79% (-5bp) on Treasury's curve, then rose back to 5.3% in Asia ahead of today's $39 billion 10-year auction and Thursday's 30-year (Reuters). FedWatch: an October hike at 21.0%, from 23.2%; December 84.7%.

OIL ROSE ON HOUTHI ATTACKS AND A GULF STORM. Brent December is $101.68 (+1.1%) and WTI November $89.81 (+0.4%). Tuesday's early slide reversed: Brent fell as much as 3.3% before settling at $100.58 (Saxo, CommodityScope). Overnight, the Houthis hit two Saudi airports (CNBC) and a storm is heading for the Gulf of Mexico (Reuters).

IRAN: TALKS STILL STALLED. Secretary of State Rubio said Iran has passed up "multiple" chances for a nuclear deal; Vice President Vance said any agreement needs a "meaningful" cut in enrichment. Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers, which now rely on US military escorts (CNBC).

FUTURES SLIP; ASIA LOWER; BITCOIN DOWN 2%. S&P 500 futures 7,853.25 (-0.26%), Nasdaq 100 futures 31,304.75 (-0.57%) as of 6:55 AM ET. The Nikkei fell 0.9%, Hong Kong 0.6% and Seoul 0.9% (AP). Bitcoin is $83,738 (-2.1%) after about $487 million of leveraged positions were liquidated (Coinomist). Gold $4,143.60 (-1.0%).

TRADE GAP WIDEST SINCE MARCH 2025. The August deficit widened to $105.6 billion, against $102.0 billion expected, as imports hit a record $420.8 billion (Reuters, BEA). Capital-goods imports rose 4.4%, a sign of AI investment (Reuters).

TODAY: FED MINUTES AT 2:00 PM. Minutes of the September 15-16 meeting, when the Fed raised rates to 3.75%-4.00%. Also: EIA oil inventories, the 10-year auction and consumer credit at 3:00 PM. Dallas Fed President Logan speaks.
client_frame_short: Stocks are at records across the board. The S&P 500 closed at its first record in two months on Tuesday, joining the Nasdaq. **The bet is on earnings: analysts expect third-quarter profits up about 30%, led by AI and energy.** Long-term Treasury yields eased a little from their 2002 highs but are still above 5.25%, so bonds remain the competition. Futures are slightly lower this morning, and oil is back above $100 after attacks on Saudi Arabia. For clients, nothing here calls for changes; today's tests are the Fed minutes at 2:00 and the 10-year auction.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, the story is records, and what they rest on.

Stocks: the S&P 500 closed at a record Tuesday, its first since August 13, and both Nasdaq indexes set records again. The rally rests on earnings: analysts expect S&P 500 profits to grow about 30% from a year earlier in the third quarter, and results start next week with the big banks. Records on earnings growth are healthier than records on hope alone.

Bonds: the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.27% Tuesday from 5.31%, its highest close since 2002. It drifted back toward 5.3% overnight ahead of today's auction. The auctions this week show how much demand there is for US debt at these levels.

Oil: Brent fell below $98 Tuesday morning, settled at $100.58, and is above $101 this morning. Gulf exports are recovering, but Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and a storm heading for the Gulf of Mexico keep supply risk alive. Iran talks remain stuck.

Growth: the trade deficit widened to $105.6 billion in August as imports hit a record, including a 4.4% jump in capital goods. That is AI spending showing up in the data. It is a sign of strong demand, though it subtracts from GDP.

The Fed: markets put October hike odds near one in five. Vice Chair Jefferson has said another hike can wait. Today's minutes show how many officials wanted to keep raising rates.

Why it matters: when stocks hit records while bonds pay over 5%, the bar for future returns rises. That is a reason for rebalancing discipline, not for selling.

For clients, the message holds: high-quality bonds pay more than 5% for a decade, an opportunity to lock in income, and long-term equity plans do not need changing. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (now 5.27%), a 30-year above 5.75% (now 5.64%), or a resumption of US strikes on Iran that sends Brent well above $105.
